newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden on collision course with Commission over alcohol.
newsitem.headline: Sweden on collision course with Commission over alcohol.

text.p: Sweden refuses to agree a deadline for ending its restrictions on the amount of alcohol people may bring home from elsewhere in the bloc, putting it on collision course with the European Commission.

European Union Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti insists that Sweden, Denmark and Finland should phase out special quotas on personal alcohol imports, saying they go against the rules of the Union's single market.
He wants a date set for when the rules will end altogether, even if he has indicated he is prepared to be flexible about when that might be.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer, much less than most other EU citizens.
Monti will meet government representatives from Stockholm, Copenhagen and Helsinki in Strasbourg, France, on Wednesday in an attempt to make progress on the sensitive issue.
"Of course, we will try to convince them," a Commission official said on Monday, adding the case may end up in the European Court of Justice if there is no deal soon.
But Sweden is in no mood to compromise.
"We agree with all the political parties that Sweden will not accept a final date" for when the rules must end, Swedish Taxation Minister Thomas Ostros said in Stockholm on Friday.
The three Nordic countries have until now presented a united front, but Denmark and Finland may be more willing to compromise.

"(They) might be willing to discuss another solution in order to avoid having a court case," one Nordic EU official said, adding this may involve a deadline beyond the year 2000 for removing the special rules.
Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict imports of cheaper alcohol, but these will expire by the end of 1996, the Commission says.

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they break the rules of the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while the Nordics want to extend them for health and tax reasons.

The issue is politically sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking. It is also a question of fiscal importance as the taxes bring in much needed revenue.
Alcohol and tobacco taxes bring in about 2.7 billion dollars annually for Sweden and 2.17 billion for Finland.

A compromise leading to a phasing out of the restrictions would gradually allow Swedes, Finns and Danes to take home more alcohol while at the same giving the three states time to prepare for the new rules, the Commission says.
But as Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict them.
Sweden's Ostros said alcohol prices would fall if Swedes were allowed to bring in large amounts. "Then we know that consumption will increase," he said.
